newsitem.title: peru: Easter brings scant hope for ending Peru crisis.
newsitem.headline: Easter brings scant hope for ending Peru crisis.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori said in comments aired on Easter Sunday that he did not foresee a quick end to Peru's 103-day hostage crisis, but insisted progress had been made to peacefully resolve the siege.
"There was a lot of speculation during Holy Week that there would be a peaceful solution but we were conscious that we were not in the final stage, that the conditions were not right," Fujimori said.

"Naturally, we are hopeful that it will be the soonest possible, but we do not glimpse a date" for an accord with Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima, he added.

His comments in an interview taped on Saturday further dampened speculation that face-to-face talks between the government and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels expected on Monday or Tuesday would lead to a break soon in Latin America's longest hostage crisis.

A tired-looking Fujimori told local TV channel Frecuencia Latina that a three-man guarantors commission mediating in the crisis would continue "preparing the ground" for a meeting between the rebels and government negotiator Domingo Palermo, but he did not say when that meeting would occur.
The two sides last met on March 12.

Fujimori sounded more optimistic than either Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto or rebel leader Nestor Cerpa, who made clear on Saturday the MRTA was insisting on its demand for the freeing of jailed comrades.
"We still don't foresee a peaceful solution soon," Cerpa said by walkie-talkie from the residence. "The positions are still not really drawing close."
He denied speculation that the MRTA had opened the way for a deal by accepting a Cuban offer of political asylum.

The dashed hopes after a week of growing optimism about a possible prompt, peaceful solution to the crisis caused the head of Peru's Roman Catholic church on Sunday to lash out at the MRTA hostage-takers in his Easter mass.
"They have lost the opportunity to show that they respect the will of the majority," Cardinal Augusto Vargas Alzamora said.

"The people are asking them to come out and instead of being generous they use arms to maintain the situation. I am saddened that Mr. Cerpa Cartolini has said that there remains much time for this to fix itself," he added. "He should learn from God and not feel superior."

It was a gloomy Easter Sunday for the hostages, who have also spent Christmas and New Year in captivity. They held a mass and got chocolate Easter eggs and fresh fruit with their usual daily supply of meals and refreshments.

In Rome, Pope John Paul II, praying for peace in his "Urbi et Orbi" message to the world, offered a special thought for the hostages. "May they finally gain the freedom they ardently long for," he said.

The captives also received a visit by guarantors Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent and Red Cross representative Michel Minnig. They stayed in the residence for close to three hours and left without speaking to reporters.
Later Cipriani met for two hours with government negotiator Palermo and then with Vincent.
In the television interview, Fujimori repeated his refusal to free jailed MRTA members. "The framework we are in ... is to not accept the release of any prisoner," he said.
But he said a special committee would continue to study pardons for Peruvians unjustly jailed on terrorism or treason charges for alleged ties to Peru's two leftist rebel groups.

Recommendations by a special panel formed before the MRTA stormed the Japanese residence on Dec. 17 led to about 100 pardons. Fujimori said the committee would recommend more pardons, but he insisted the hostage crisis "has nothing to do with the liberation of those unjustly condemned."
He also said his government was working to improve jail conditions, another main concern of rebels who say their comrades are condemned to slow deaths in virtual "tombs."
Among the hostages are the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia, Fujimori's brother Pedro, two cabinet ministers, military officers and Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
